hero.title: Ultra-light travel gear for the modern explorer.
hero.text: ULT Gear was a one-person product lab: about thirty ideas for gear I wished existed, taken as far as tech packs, factory samples and prototypes before the math caught up. This is what got built.

idea.title: Three tribes, one bag
idea.text: Ultralight backpacking, digital nomads, minimalist travel. Three groups buying the same kind of gear from three different aisles. ULT Gear sat in the overlap: one small backpack, ultra-packable clothing, and accessories that disappear when you're not using them.

materials.title: Materials and testing
materials.text: Before designing anything technical I tested what already existed: staining and cleaning tests, heating and drying tests, packing and wrinkle tests. Fabric swatches in 50D and 75D, sample orders laid out on the bed, packing layouts to see what a one-bag kit really looks like, and sketches of what a heated system might be.

storefront.title: Before the products, a store
storefront.text: ULT Gear launched in 2023 as a curated shop of the best ultralight gear already on the market, with the plan to swap in ULT Gear's own designs as they came off the line. The store ran; the line never came off the line.

ending.title: How it ended
paras: I had about thirty products I wanted. Yes, I know that's insane. That's just how my mind works.

I took many of these ideas well past the design phase. I worked with clothing and shoe designers to build tech packs, had fabric samples shipped from specialty shops, used a 3D-print shop for hardware components, and a product-design company for the more technical ideas. I built real prototypes for many of them, some of which I still use today, others I can only laugh at.

But all of these ideas ran into the same problem: cost. A single shoe mold costs about $10k, and a usable prototype would have been $20k minimum. Custom 3D-printed parts were in the thousands just to design. Specialty fabrics were a nightmare to source, and manufacturers had minimum order quantities in the thousands. By the time I added it all up, I was staring down $15k to $25k just to produce one size of a single product.
Maybe people learn this in business school. I learned it in the real world, and for that, I am moderately grateful.

site.partners: Product designers in Atlanta. A 3D print shop in Denver. Manufacturers in China. Material sourcers in Switzerland. Two shoe designers. One clothing designer.

t: I started with clothing because it seemed like the simplest. I wanted one of everything: ULT-branded hoodies, shirts, shorts, socks. Quick-dry, anti-wrinkle, anti-stain, built-in packing pockets, multiple zippered pockets. Basically every feature I look for in travel gear, in every piece of clothing, tailored to minimalist travel.

I learned about tech packs, material sourcing and MOQs. Some ideas died because I couldn't find or get the materials I wanted. Some died because I found existing products already doing it better. Some died because it's nearly impossible to express a clear idea to a manufacturer through text and images, and US-based manufacturing was too expensive. Many died from minimum order quantities. Shipping played a role too: sending material samples and prototypes back and forth meant two to three months for a single prototype, so improvements and iterations would have taken years.

t: At the same time I worked on a few backpack, day pack and sling bag concepts, and ran into the same issues: rare, unavailable or prohibitively expensive materials, long wait times, and existing brands that weren't perfect but already had recognition and a cult following. These died for similar reasons.

t: I had a number of physical product concepts too, and pursued a few: ultralight waterproof clip-on bags, a security belt that combined my favorite travel features (no metal, stretchy cloth, hidden security pockets), an ultra-portable drying rack for the perennial problem of nowhere to hang clothes in hotels and hostels, a packable picnic and beach blanket, a free-standing toiletry bag for hostel bathrooms with no counter space, and a packable wash basin for doing laundry in the sink.

I followed a similar path: product designers in Atlanta, a 3D print shop in Denver, manufacturers in China, material sourcers in Switzerland. The same constraints came up. Rare materials, manufacturing minimums, long prototyping timelines, and the cost of prototypes and components.

t: A number of concepts were technical: a packable heating pad for drying clothes, a packable heated hanger, heated clothing in general, a portable ultrasonic cleaner for washing clothes. Some required technology I knew existed in other products, but I wasn't sure I could adapt it to mine. So I started by testing existing products to see if they worked as advertised: staining and cleaning tests, heating and drying tests, packing and wrinkle tests.

I spent a good amount of time figuring out what was possible, technically and legally. Could I license certain tech? Could I change something enough that it wasn't patent infringement? Did I need patents? Did patents already exist? For many of these, most of the work was finding out whether the concept was possible and worth pursuing.

t: One project I spent a lot of time on was SwitchKicks. Shoes have always been a problem for travelers. At minimum you need sandals, hiking shoes and casual shoes on the road, and ideally a dressier pair, a higher-ankle hiking shoe, and a cold-weather shoe if your travels cross climates. So I wondered whether I could build a layered shoe system: a minimalist base shoe for the beach or barefoot running, with slip-on layers that change the utility or the style. Colored patterns and materials for looks, an adjustable base for traction.

I worked with a couple of shoe designers to get the concept down. It died when I learned a single shoe mold, one size of one style, runs $10k to $12k. For a concept built on a flexible base plus layers plus materials plus outsoles, that meant something like $500k to $1M in R&D before anyone could try one on.

concepts.title: Minimalist Barefoot Sandals

t: All of the ideas died from cost, time, and the slow realization that I was building for a market of one: me. I do believe I could have found customers and built a new market. But without a lot of money, it was never going to happen.

products.title: Packable Travel Shorts
products.summary: Quick-dry shorts that roll into their own back pocket.
products.story: The spec I sent the factory: anti-bacterial quick-dry fabric as thin as swim trunks, two indented zippered side pockets, and one centered back pocket with a double-sided zipper so the shorts pack into themselves. Elastic waistband with a no-show drawstring, elastic belt hooks, a printed tag instead of a sewn one, and an inner hook for hanging. Black, 9-inch inseam. Two sample rounds came back. V2 fixed the waistband, the drawstrings and the belt loops, and I measured every pocket against the shorts I actually travel with.
wanted: Anti-bacterial, lightweight, quick-dry fabric, as thin as swim trunks
Two zippered side pockets, slightly indented, not on the side seam
One centered back pocket with a double-sided zipper, so the shorts pack into it
Elastic waistband with an inner drawstring, plus elastic belt hooks
Tagless, with care instructions printed and an inner hook for hanging
docs: Factory spec and correspondence
V2 revision notes, annotated photos

products.title: Packable Travel Pants
products.summary: The pants version of the shorts, with ankle zips so they come off over shoes.
products.story: 90% polyester, 10% spandex in the waistband. Two indented zippered side pockets, a double-sided back zipper pocket big enough to pack the pants into, an inner drawstring, belt loops, and ankle-high zippers so they open and come off without taking your shoes off. Tagless, with a hook for hanging. Samples came back in black. The pocket bags were the first thing I turned inside out.
wanted: Ankle zippers so the pants come off over shoes
Reversible back pocket that doubles as the packing pocket
Belt loops and an inner drawstring, so they work with or without the belt
docs: Factory spec and correspondence

products.title: Ultralight Packable Hoodie
products.summary: A grid-polyester hoodie with a stuff pocket in the upper back, so it packs into itself.
products.story: Designed with Summit Prototyping & Design: a lightweight polyester hoodie with a grid pattern, a half zipper, thumb gaiters, and a pocket sewn into the upper back so the whole thing packs into itself. Men's and women's tech packs, version 1.0, dated June 5, 2023. Before that I bought and lived in the hoodies I admired, KETL and Kühl, to steal the details that mattered: the hanging hook, where the stuff pocket goes, how small they packed.
docs: Men's and women's tech packs, v1.0, 13 pages each, June 2023
Design contract with Summit Prototyping & Design, April 2023

products.title: Ultralight T-Shirt
products.summary: The companion piece to the hoodie, from the same design round.
products.story: A packable ultralight tee, men's tech pack v1.0 from the same June 2023 round as the hoodie. This is where the apparel line hit the wall: the factory's minimum order was 1,000 units, or 250 each across four styles in one color, men's and women's, four sizes. Fine for a brand. Not fine for one person testing an idea.
docs: Men's tech pack, v1.0, June 2023
Minimum-order correspondence

products.title: Hidden Pocket Travel Belt
products.status: Samples in hand · two design rounds
products.summary: A stretch belt with two zip-sealed hidden pockets and a buckle that stays out of the way.
products.story: A stretch belt with two hidden pockets, a low-profile plastic buckle, and a side adjuster so the pockets never sit under the buckle. I annotated every revision for the factory: where each pocket starts, how the fabric wraps the buckle, and three closure options (an outside zipper, a top zipper, an inside zip-lock). Two rounds of samples came back, then a third design around a double-sided zipper. Two travel products in one, which was the whole point.
wanted: Two hidden pockets, one either side of the buckle, ~38 x 100 mm each
Single low-profile buckle, 5.3 mm, push-button release
Belt-size adjuster moved to the side so it never fights the pockets
docs: Design V1 and V2 annotation sets
Double-sided zipper design

products.title: SwitchKicks
products.summary: Modular travel shoes: one lightweight inner shoe, swappable outer shells.
products.story: A sandal-like base shoe that fits inside a thin minimalist shell, with outer shells you swap to change the shoe: sandal or beach, dress, house or lounger, athletic or runner. I hired a footwear designer on a phased ideation process, 14 hours for the base shoe and four uppers, then critique rounds, and got a 25-page travel-footwear brief plus three first-round concepts with lace and laceless inner shoes, mesh, canvas and suede outers, and one-piece EVA soles. A single shoe mold costs about $10k and a usable prototype would have been $20k minimum. That is where it stopped.
docs: Travel Footwear design brief, 25 pages, May 2023
SwitchKicks first-round concept designs, 3 concepts
Phased design invoice: ideation, critique, ideation

products.title: Packable Day Pack
products.summary: The one that got furthest: factory samples with the ULT Gear mark.
products.story: Factory samples in gray and blue with the ULT Gear mark, a double-sided zipper so the whole pack folds into its own top pocket, and a second round with the interior pocket moved and the strap keepers fixed. Real prototypes, in hand, tested on real trips.
wanted: Folds into its own top pocket through a double-sided zipper
Interior zip pocket relocated after round one
Branded label on the pocket and the packed pouch
docs: Two sample rounds with annotated revisions

products.title: Packable Waist Pack
products.summary: Same idea, smaller: a waist pack that zips into its own pocket.
products.story: The day pack's little sibling. Two samples from the same factory, both packing into their own pocket.

products.title: Security Chest Sling
products.summary: A packable anti-theft sling that sits flat against the chest.
products.story: A packable anti-theft sling with the pocket opening against the body, so nobody else can open it. It started as my own sketches and ended as a spec drawing from a designer: 10.5 by 5.25 inches, packs into its own pouch through the bottom zipper, with a ladder-lock or buckle slider on the strap.
docs: Design drawing with packable view and hardware options

products.title: Universal Drying Rack
products.summary: A clothes-drying rack that collapses into a tube the size of a phone tripod.
products.story: The product I chased longest. Wire hangers, snake-arm brackets, three rounds of 3D-printed connectors, carbon-fiber rods, and a photo-tripod base from Ulanzi as the platform. The drawing shows the goal: a hanging rack that folds down like a kaleidoscope tube. I got an injection-molding overview from Protolabs for the connector. Custom 3D-printed parts ran into the thousands just to design properly, and that was the end of the road.
wanted: Collapses into a tube, like a portable phone stand
Hangs from a door, a rail or a tripod base
Holds a full load of hand-washed clothes
docs: Protolabs injection-molding overview
Pole layout drawing, v2.0

products.title: Packable Wash Basin
products.summary: A 10-liter wash basin that packs down to a 6 by 16 cm pouch.
products.story: A foldable basin for washing clothes on the road without a sink: 10 liters, 70D ripstop over a PU-coated waterproof liner, two carrying handles, a bottom handle for emptying, and a zippered pocket sewn into the edge so the whole thing packs down to a pouch. I tested an off-the-shelf basin in the sink first, then spec'd V1 and a modified V2 with a carrying case.
wanted: 10 L capacity, lightweight waterproof fabric
Zippered pocket on the edge so it packs into itself
Packs to roughly 6 x 16 cm
docs: V1 spec, four pages
V2 spec with fabric types and carrying case

products.title: Packable Beach Blanket
products.summary: A pocket blanket that stuffs into its own corner pocket.
products.story: A ground blanket that stuffs into its own corner pocket. I bought and tested the best of the category before deciding whether there was room for ULT Gear to improve on it.

products.title: Heated Drying: Pad, Hanger, Towel
products.status: Patent searches · bench tests · design proposal
products.summary: A packable heating pad for drying clothes, plus a heated hanger, heated towel and heated clothing.
products.story: A family of ideas around one problem: wet clothes and towels in a hostel room with nowhere to dry them. A packable heating pad you lay clothes on. A packable heated hanger. A towel with carbon-fiber heating elements and a magnetic wireless charging tag. Heated clothing in general. Some of it needed technology I knew existed in other products, and I wasn't sure I could adapt it to mine, so I started by testing what was already out there: heating and drying tests on a bench, including a food dehydrator with a pair of socks in it and an off-the-shelf heating mat with a load of laundry on it. I ran automated prior-art searches in January and February 2023, got a research-and-ideation proposal from a product design firm, and spent most of the time on the legal questions: could I license the tech, could I change it enough to avoid a patent, did I need patents of my own. The same searches covered a USB-powered belt as a portable power source for heated clothing. None of it went further than the bench.
docs: Prior-art search reports, January and February 2023
Research and ideation proposal from a product design firm
Bench tests: heating mat with laundry, dehydrator with socks

products.title: Portable Ultrasonic Cleaner
products.summary: Could a pocket-size ultrasonic cleaner do laundry in a hostel sink?
products.story: Ultrasonic cleaners exist for jewelry and glasses. I wanted to know whether a small one could wash clothes in a sink or a packable basin. So I ran staining and cleaning tests: stained fabric squares in two bowls of water, one with the cleaner running and one without, then laid the squares out on a tray to compare. It was the same question as the heated gear, whether technology that already existed for something else could be adapted to travel laundry, and it stayed on the bench for the same reasons.
wanted: Small enough to pack, powered by USB
Cleans a sink-load of clothes without a machine
docs: Staining and cleaning test photos
